Question: What are the advantages of CRM in the airline industry?
Answer: Simply put CRM is like the engine oil to an engine. It stands for Crew Resource Management. Every airline has CRM training as one of its yearly mandatory training to highlight the importance of clear communication as well as equally important barriers to it. An efficient CRM training is supposed to showcase the importance of the crew being alert at all times in-flight. Not only in terms of presence of mind but also foresee certain avoidable events and keep them from happening. A simple example would be, A passenger on a relatively empty flight is requesting for a lot of alcohol and in quick succession. A crew set with good CRM training would not only identify the passenger by his seat number but also but his looks and what he is wearing incase he changes his seat to ask another crew for alcohol. Another related example would be, everytime this passenger leaves his seat (if he does) to go to the lavatory, crew responsible for that area would be make a mental note of how long its been since the person has not been seen in his seat and I considerable times has passed then alert the fellow crew and check where this person is. S/he can be passed out In a lavatory or smoking in a toilet (it has happened). Fellow crew members feel free to add to this interesting topic.

Question: How do I make six figures working for myself?
Answer: In my opinion its because of my ability to keep pushing myself to come upto the expectations of my customers (and sometimes even beyond that) who have paid lump-sum amounts to be safely flown from one point to another. In my training to become a fight attendant I've been trained on how to deal with a whole lot of life threatening scenarios which can take place even on a normal day and normal flight. These scenarios have taken place in the past without giving people a chance to realise what was happening before it was too late, hence these forseable situations are included in our training telling us what should we do and what actions to be taken to minimise casualty in the following situations which are as follows Apart from the safety & security aspect, I've been also trained to attend to medical emergencies ranging from fractures, nose bleeds, severe ear aches and headaches to epilepsy, cardiac arrest and even delivering a baby in-flight and other minor medical situations like sprains and strains n the likes of it. Coming to the service point of view, I must confess that I have been honoured to meet some exceptional personalities on board which have actually inspired me to become a better person and I thank them for that. Also I have come across a few individuals who just want to complain for every thing around them in order to get attention first then eventually some compensation but then there are such people in each and every corner of the world. Surprisingly I've also come across individuals who for their own comfort won't upright their seat even for a pregnant lady to have her dinner in peace. Supposedly adults who have spoken very derogatory and harsh words for some things as simple as an extra piece bread. To handle all of them and even few whose behaviour goes beyond logical explanations and to do that with a patient mind and a calm & composed attitude is what makes my employers consider to pay me the said salary. I can easily ignore a call bell or the timid “excuse me” I thought I heard but I choose not to; reason being - KARMA. I understand and respect this worldwide proven phenomenon of “what goes around comes around”. When I'm at my wits ends by the end of 15 hours flight & an adult asks me for a glass of water just before when I was about to sit for landing, instead of rolling my eyes I think (I do that inside my head :-P ) I think ‘what if it was my mother/father?’ and have always given that last glass with a smile even if it's a tight lipped one. If its a kid then I like to think that one day when my kid does something similar maybe this deed of mine will ensure him/her a similar or better reaction in future. Alot of my colleagues who I personally know go above and beyond their limits to do the same and I'm glad to have learnt from them the art of keeping calm & getting the job done.

Question: Do flight attendants ever get tips from first class passengers for exemplary service?
Answer: I was galley manager on that flight from London to a particular city in middle east. I had heard my supervisor brief us that we are expecting a VVIP group (members of the royal family) travelling with us. I thought nothing much of it as it's quite usual on that route. Somewhere middle of the flight I went in the cabin to check with customers who are awake if they would wanna get some beverages or snacks. While getting to know how their flight was going, I got into a conversation with this lady and came to know that they are bringing in her 11 years old little brother back from London after 3 years where he was admitted for cancer. He was 8 years when he was admitted and had a machine fixed somewhere in his lungs to help him breath which was finally removed a few months ago. It would be after 3 years that he would be sleeping in his own bed in his own house without any nurse or doctor supervising him once in a while and without any life support machines surrounding him. That hit me hard. So I went to galley and made a special dessert presentation plate for this kid which said, “Welcome back home, Live Long Life.” I checked with the lady if it's okay for him to consume the contents of that presentation plate and she gave us a thumbs up. It was just chocolate cake and some fruits. Somewhere in between I believe I saw her wipe some tears as well. The young man was super excited to have all the crew come up to him with the chocolate goodies and stuff and licked the plate clean within minutes. We felt happy and blessed to be able to make his flight home a little more special for him and that was it for us. At least for me. In about 5 minutes I got a call bell from that lady and went to check on her. She extended her hand and told me, “thank you for doing what you did, he is very happy” and the way she held her hand I knew she was holding onto something which she wanted to give me and I politely thanked her for her gesture and took a small step back to hint that I would have to decline her kind gift as it's not allowed by our airline to accept any tips. I folded my hands in Namaste and just as I was about to leave I saw her facial expressions change to somewhat disappointment and hurt. In a fraction of a second the sweet and calm in her eyes changed to confusion and hurt. I knew it then that that refusal of mine hurt her sentiments so to i went ahead and accepted what she was offering and upon going back to my galley realised it's the highest value currency note of this particular country which is almost about 150 usd. I immediately went back to her to tell her that I cannot accept it as it's a very big amount but she was just not ready to listen. I thanked her for her generosity and holding on to something which serves as a reminder of having made a positive impact on someone's life at that moment made me very happy. Till date I have never considered it as a currency note. It's more like an emotional note with good memory to it. Eventually I accepted it and to this day have it in my file of achievements along with other certificates of excellence. I hope I never have to use it ever. Coming back to the flight, we landed, parked and opened doors to see 4 Audis with a brigade of chauffeurs waiting to receive this particular family. They bid farewell and the lady again thanked us one more time before bidding farewell. Best wishes.

English proficiency: they would be checking your command over English by way of fill-in-the-blanks for simple paragraphs, match the columns to the best suited words with their meaning and to summarize a full page story into 5 or 10 lines. Basic maths: youll be asked to answer 5th grade word problems such as , “ the river's downhill current is 10 km/hr, you are at the base of the 15 km river bed and need to boat until the middle of it. Your boat can cover 5 km/hr in the current scenario. Calculate how much time you'd take to reach the centre”. Debate: Be respectable and confident while you are at it. Don't be rowdy and don’t try to dominate. Listen attentively, add your views where necessary, appreciate logical points and dont intervene someone, if someone intervenes you then calmly and assertively say “I would have appreciated if you allowed me to make my point, you can continue after me”. Group discussion: you'll get brownie points to start the discussion and with each positive gesture you'll add up on these points. Listening attentively, appreciating valid points of others, being composed and calm while contributing your own points and when asking someone who's kept mum throughout the process if they would like to add something to the discussion. Generally just be nice. 2 mins speech: you might be asked to speak for 2 mins about your hobby, city, aviation and it's related topics, your debate topic or even the topic of your group discussion. Use simple words to convey your thoughts, don't try to be highyl articulate if it doesn't come naturally to you. Final interview: they'll ask you questions such as: All the best and one more advice is to sit in front of the mirror and practice your self introduction for 30 mins everyday starting from atleast a week before the interview.

Question: Is it true that a flight crew has to be able to evacuate a plane in 90 seconds? How do you get a group of panicking people to cooperate?
Answer: Scene 1: Mr. M (safety instructor): guys I'm gonna give you a scenario and i want you'll to act as if it were real. You have permission to use whatever means you deem fit to make me move out of the aircraft. Your goal is to make me move. That's it. Once you'll are done then I'll show you how it's supposed to be done but first I wanna see what limits are you ready to go to to get this job done. Scene 2: (A life size replica of internal of an Airbus 320 aircraft is provided by the manufacturer and the trainer is seated in the emergency exit, each one of us is given a chance to make him move and he's going to act all shocked and frozen; only one person acts as the operating crew n the rest 19 of us are oberservers to the scenario) Scenario - Normal day, normal landing, 500 feet before landing, pilot-not-flying announces BRACE BRACE. Aircraft crashes and comes to complete hault, you see a big fire at the back end of aircraft and thick dense smoke filling the interior, the passengers on the emergency exit have gone in shock and froze to even remember the breifing given during securing of the cabin, you as a crew member have to first make them move away so you can reach the exit and open it and shout your commands,GO! Almost everyone from my group were shouting at top of their voices to make the instructor move but he's just sitting in the middle seat (window & aisle is empty) gripping the armrests, eyes wide as saucers and jaws dropped down. We tried making quick hand movements, some tried shaking him from his shoulders, one even tried pulling his arms but none succeded. Everyone of us gave up while trying different phrases and decent tactics to make him move when he told us that all of us would have failed if it was an exam. Then the instructor choose the 3 biggest guys in our group each more than 6′ and made them sit on the emergency exits giving them instructions to try and grip the armrests as tightly as possible. He repeated the scenario and in 2 seconds after yelling GO! he got the one sitting in aisle out by pulling him from his shirt’s collar and tearing it from the collar, if I remember correctly then 2 of his buttons made a projectile exit from the demonstration scene, for the second one he made a death grip around the neck with his arm while using his other hand to grip the armrest on the aisle and succeeded in 3 seconds to have him standing in the aisle, the 3rd one by now was bewildered by what he witnessed (the rest 17 of us had almost similar expressions of disbelief) and was about to get up and leave when the instructor motioned him to hold the armrest tightly, as he did the instructor raised his arms in sir as if he's about to give my bacthmate a tight slap but stopped a couple of centimeters away and went ahead to pull him away from the emergency exit before opening the exit and shouting instructions to evacuate. We were dumbfounded how our 60 years old supposedly decent and articulate German instructor turned into this aggressive beast of a man. While he was neatly arranging his clothing he called the first guy to check the size of the torn shirt behind his neck and as he tried reaching the tag this batchmate of mine still shaken ducked still under the shock of what just happened. The batch went crazy this time howling and laughing. I'm less than 30 seconds our instructor was back with a new crisp shirt and asked my batchmate to change once the class was over. His message was clear. Use any means necessary, by force or by getting physical, as long as it makes the passengers do as they are told to to save their lives every tactic is allowed. The guy showed up in his new shirt the next day and wore it only that day as he wants to keep both the shirts as both a reminder and a souvenir. After I started flying I came to know that it was pretty normal to end up tearing the shirt or a blouse hence they maintained stocks of shirts & blouses for men n women respectively. Thanks for reading.

Question: As a cabin crew member, what are your funniest experiences with first-time travelers?
Answer: It usually gets funny when the aircraft goes through turbulence. For the first timers its almost a que for them to start reciting their holy prayers, remember freinds and family and in the gulf or islamic countires ask help from the almighty by screaming his name loudly “ALLAH”. We were going to one of the cities in pakistan, multan. The captain had told the cabin crew that prior to landing we can expect it to be ‘‘quite bumpy’’ as its very usual on that route especially in summers. So we completed the cabin secure procedures earlier than the normal n took our seats for landing. Now my jumpseat was directly facing the passengers and opposite to me seated were 3 gentlemen. The one in the middle i suppose was travelling for the first time as he kept looking awkwardly outsode the window and kept asking how much time before we touch down every 2 minutes or so. Now just before the landing gears were to be deployed we started experiencing turbulence and although the others were taken by surprise with the first 1 meter (or so) dive te aircraft took, thia particular gentleman in the middle screamt on top of his voice “YAAA ALLLLAAAAAHHHHHH” and almost gave a heart attack to his fellow passengers, me included. The passenger sitting on the aisle besides him was an old guy maybe in his 60s, almost threw himself on the aisle. I remember almost everybody having a go at that guy as a revenge but understood in seconds the plight of this gentleman and carried on with whatever they were doing. Little did they knew that this was not over yet. Then came the second bump which was comparatively smaller than the first but i saw this guy in the middle dig his fingers in the knees of the guys seated on either sides of him and almost stand up in his seat to get over the feeling of weightlessness. It didnt help and actually made it worse as he was pulled back in his seat the moment aircraft made a correction within fraction of a second and regained that 1/2 meter drop. “YAAAAAA ALLLLLLAAAAAHHHHHHH” he screamt again and this time didnt stop here. As if he could already see god, he started making his confessions loudly and with shorter and shorter breaths. I could understand what he said so here is the translation “oh lord almighty! Please have mercy on me n my family. I will pray all 5 times from here on if you let me live. I will not look at another women if you let me live. I will not even think about alcohol if you let me live. Please oh please oh dear almighty, forgive me for my sins and if i am to meet you today theb show me the gates of heaven!” All the while me n his fellow passengers tried to calm him down but nothing helped! The moment the aircraft touched down he wanted to get off that damned machine he said. Till this day i remeber the look on his face. Im glad he didnt have a heart attack. The rest of the passengers were all smiles and nods while disembarking and a few handshakes with a laugh as well. May God bless him and give him either smooth skies or the strength to undergo turbulence.

Question: What are the different qualities of a cabin crew?
Answer: First and foremost is being able to remain calm and composed to assess a situation and act accordingly. It can be anything from handling a very demanding passenger to a medical case on-board or even preparing the passengers for a crash landing. Also being vigilant and knowing what's not normal is important. Once during service our aircraft was flying over the ocean and quite suddenly I realised a very unusual vibration throughout the fuselage causing weird creeking noises, immediately i called up flight deck and it turned out the Pilot-in-command (PIC) had given full control to one of the trainee pilot who was increasing the altitude of the aircraft at an incredible speed and that too at quite a steep angle thus increasing the drag and causing the vibrations. Cabin crew are the eyes and ears and nose of the flight deck, anything we see hear or smell that is unusual we need to inform the PIC. Thinking of the top of your head and being able to act quickly is another trait that's very much needed in this job. Incase of a medical emergency when your colleague needs you to get a medical kit, oxygen and help, you really have to be fast as every passing second is important. And of course being able to smile at all points of customer interaction is a great deal for the hiring airlines.

Question: What is the difference between check in and cabin bag?
Answer: Cabin baggage - it's usually a smaller dimension trolley or a bag which can conveniently be stowed in the hatracks or overhead compartment or under the seat in front of you. In most airlines it usually has a limit of being 7 or 8 KGS at the most. It's allowed in the cabin hence the name. Checked-in baggage - the suitcases and big bags which you literally have to check them in for the flight (example: you yourself checking into a hotel whereas in this case it's your bags in place of you n it's a flight In place of a hotel) and you receive a small baggage tag which corresponds to the baggage tag stuck on your suitcases n bags n has information about your final destination where you'll be receiving it after clearing immigration. Question: What are the weirdest things flight attendants have seen in their line of duty?
Answer: Well the weirdest/scariest thing I've witnessed on board an aircraft was having a near death experience on a single aisle aircraft. I'm seated on the right side of the cabin facing passengers and it's a normal 45 mins flight. Around 50-60 seconds after take off suddenly the aircraft tips to its left...hard left..so much so that I realised my hands quickly moving to grab my 4 point harness over my chest to prevent myself from hanging weirdly from my jump seat. Everything after that moment was like a slow motion movie. I remember having a quick glance at my crew seated on the adjacent door and I saw her eyes wide open and almost gasping for breath and simultaneously pushing her body away from the door as she was almost falling off on to it due to gravity. I heard someone in particular scream, a guy voice, "oh Lord!!" and in a fraction of a second I had these pictures of my family and friends and even my ex-gfs flash in front of my eyes like a continuous flow of a powerpoint presentation. As the aircraft had banked to its extreme left and literally its left wing pointing straight towards the sea we were flying on I could see a few unsecured loose objects falling off towards the left of the fuselage and colliding with seat's head rest before falling on the left side. In particular I remember seeing something that I believe was an i-pad falling off and started rotating at a crazy speed after hitting one of its edge on the headrest and thumping on one of the windows. All this happened within a short span of 4-5 seconds before the aircraft started aligning to a rather normal position. After a good 5 mins the captain gave us the signal by switching the seatbelt sign off n on that it was safe for Crew to move for the snacks service but my legs felt weak and were trembling until we landed. Later we learned from the captain that he was forced to take that maneuver in order to avoid getting into a mid-air collision path with a double deck AIRBUS 380. As ours was a way smaller aircraft it was easier for it to have had made that maneuver faster compared to the A-380. We didn't bother to ask how it was possible, was it the ATC's fault or the A-380's or what went wrong as we were just thankful to be alive that day and grateful to the flightdeck crew's decision. Myself and the crew did not see even 1 passenger on that flight went to use the washroom. Snacks were barely and I mean barely consumed that day. Part and parcel of crew life.
